عد 1771 فلم THE CLOUD- CAPPED STAR مخرج Ritwik Ghatak فلــــــم من بنگلادش، جميل ناحيه التصوير والدفئ الذي يخلق الاسود والابيض للمـــــــشهد والمُشاهد من عشاق افلام الاسود والابيض، قصه الفلم جمــــيله ولكن تطور الاحداث بهذه الصيغه المبالغ بها يجعلك تنفر من الفلم، كـــذلك (خبطه الاداءالمسرحي) للممثلين من ضمن عيوب هذا الفلم، واذا هناك حســـــــنه فيه فهي تصويره الرائع والزوايا التي تستقر فيها الكاميــــرا. وانقل لكم كلمه من محب للسينما شاهد الفلم فقال: كل شخص محب للسينما ولم يتابع هذه التحفه فهو يحمل عار!!!!! ولا ادري اين العار في عدم مشاهدتي لفلم اغلبه مبالغه غير مقنعه سواء للحدث او الاداء. يحــــكي فيلم "Meghe Dhaka Tara" القصة المأساوية لابنة جميلة لعائلة لاجئة من الطبقة المتوســـــــــــطة من شرق باكستان، تعيش في ضواحي كلكتا في ظـــــل ظروف متواضعة، تضحي نيتا بكل شيء من أجل أســـرتها، بما في ذلك سعادتها الشخصية، وأموالها، وصحتها، بينما نادرًا ما يتم الاعتراف بإنجازاتها من قبل الأشخاص من حولها. فلم THE CLOUD- CAPPED STAR مخرج Ritwik Ghatak انتاج 1960 وقت 126 دقيقه تمثيل Supriya Choudhury، Anil Chatterjee جائزة 1 ترشح

Indian Neo-Realism mixed with melodrama. It's a combination of identifiers that sends shivers down my spine, and the film doesn't disappoint. It's a sluggish, 2-hour-long social drama (with some horrible musical influences) that never redeems itself, but only gets worse as it progresses. A relatively well-off family flees from their home and ends up in the slums of Calcutta. The daughter of the family does her very best to improve the situation for her family, even sacrificing her own life and happiness to do so. For all the sacrifices she makes though, her family doesn't seem very appreciative of her efforts. A film about self-sacrifice where things just get worse for the lead character. The performances aren't that great, the cinematography is very basic and the drama piles up endlessly. The music was pretty grating too, making the 2-hour runtime a real obstacle. Not my type of film, I really disliked this one.

La cinematografía es tan pero tan buena que ha hecho creer a la gente que la película es extraordinaria. Sinceramente no es nada más que una telenovela ramplona; si la historia se desarrollara en México no sería más que un capítulo de Lo que Callamos las Mujeres , o de Mujeres Casos de la Vida Real, o de La Rosa de Guadalupe. ¿Acaso tiene trama la historia? Digo, porque ver a la protagonista ser una abnegada magdalena que sufre y sufre por espacio de dos horas no es nada interesante. El problema de Ritwik Ghatak es que si quiere hablar del papel de la mujer dentro de una sociedad misógina, lo termina arruinando porque romantiza el sufrimiento de la protagonista; si Ghatak quiere hablar de los efectos socioeconómicos de la infame Partición, pues no entiendo porque no lo aborda en lo absoluto y la película fácilmente puede prescindir de eso. Todos los personajes son caricaturas. Muchos admiran la actuación de Supriya Choudhury, pero, para mí, no tiene nada de rango y se nota rumbo al final cuando a su personaje le da tuberculosis (aparte de todo lo que la familia y novio le hacen le da tuberculosis; nada más faltó que regresaran los británicos y la hicieran esclava o algo así) y ella está re-tiesa. Bastante decepcionante trabajo si pensamos en lo que también estaba haciendo Satyajit Ray en ese entonces.

This is one of those infuriating melodramas that spends two hours documenting the suffering experienced by a saintly young woman with a drab personality. She is surrounded by selfish monsters who don't bear any resemblance to actual human beings and the screenplay works overtime to make us feel pity for the idiotic masochist at the centre of the story. They presumably intended to craft this tale into a feminist parable about the horrors of a sexist society but it ends up falling prey to all sorts of misogynistic clichés. It's telling that every single female character who is presented is an unsympathetic light is willing to push back against social boundaries. The only woman that we are asked to admire is a pushover who actively chooses to become a martyr. I'm sick of watching supposedly tragic dramas that tell stories about characters who suffer from inertia.

Upon my initial viewing of Ritwk Ghatak’s The Cloud-Capped Star last year, I wrote extensively about this film’s larger role in analyzing the socio-economic contexts in which the film emerged out of and how these factors, although never expressly called out in the film, convey a theme of industrialization and modernization as a method of disrupting the personal lives and social intimacies of those in society. While this is an analysis that I still stand by and continue to be proud of, I do want to highlight another aspect of the film that I neglected on my first watch; this being a review of the film itself. The Cloud-Capped Star is a difficult film to sit through both due to its themes and the structure of the film itself. This is a film that is poorly structured and paced causing it to be monotonous to watch given its over two hour runtime. Due to the language barrier I cannot attest to the quality of the performances, but there is an aura of over-exaggeration to the way characters move around their environments. This makes the performances feel very stilted and performative, which comes across as soap operatic rather than melodramatic. This is certainly a by-product of casting mostly non-actors however that doesn’t make it any less jarring to watch. In the end, The Cloud-Capped Star is a film which I appreciate for its narrative scope and underlying societal critiques more than I appreciate it as a film to watch and enjoy in its own right.

5.5 DVD The first of Ritwik Ghatak’s films that I have seen (and as I understand it, his most well-known, certainly outside India), The Cloud-Capped Star is a film which has considerable aesthetic beauty, but sadly the simplistic, overwrought melodrama failed to hold my interest through its (excessive) two-hour running time. In terms of visuals, the opening scene in particular is an absolute stunner: our protagonist, Neeta (Supriya Choudhury) walks toward the camera, emerging from beneath the bows of a majestic tree (the camera placed far enough away that its entire massive frame is within shot).  As she draws level with a man singing by the adjacent riverbank (we subsequently learn that this is her brother, Shankar (Anil Chatterjee)), the camera angle changes to a sensational deep focus shot, showing Neeta in close up, Shankar in the middle-distance and finally a train whooshing past in the background.  Whilst nothing in the rest of the film can quite match the brilliance or flamboyance of this opening, Ghatak’s skill as a director (and presumably also Dinen Gupta as cinematographer) is clear throughout the film in terms of the blocking, lighting and framing of each scene, the intimacy and down-to-earth simplicity of which draw clear comparisons to the Italian neorealists, Satyajit Ray’s Apu trilogy and even the Japanese masters Mizoguchi, Naruse and Ozu. At a story level, unfortunately, I am less enthused.  The plot revolves around Neeta and her family, who live in poverty in the suburbs of Calcutta.  The family are refugees from Pakistan, who were forced to flee following Partition (the film doesn’t seem to make any explicit reference to Partition, although I’m sure that a viewer with more knowledge of the history would pick up on more of the implied references than I).  Neeta is the only person in the family who makes a decent wage; she tries to balance being the breadwinner with persevering with her college studies, however finds it increasingly difficult to do so when her family and even her own fiancée refuse to get jobs themselves, preferring instead to leach off the good-natured Neeta so that they can prioritise their own selfish ambitions. The first third of the film is quite interesting, with Ghatak using the classic trick of filmmakers such as Ray and Ozu of dropping the viewer into another world without exposition or any other form of hand-holding.  This means that the audience has to work out piece by piece who everyone is in relation to everyone else as information is gradually provided, an approach that I find very rewarding when done correctly.  However, after this set-up, The Cloud-Capped Star becomes increasingly and distractingly melodramatic, with misfortune after misfortune heaped upon the protagonist as the film devolves (slowly, agonisingly slowly) into an exercise in brow-beating moralism.  It doesn’t help that without exception the characters are absurdly simplistic: from Neeta, who is little more than a self-sacrificing martyr, to her intensely unlikeable, over-the-top mother to her fiancée, a weak and self-centered man who ends up having an affair with Neeta’s sister.  There is no nuance to any of these characters or the narrative in general (the family’s absurd level of cruelty towards Neeta seems designed simply to provide a contrast with Neeta’s uncomplicated wholesomeness), and as a result the film feels a million miles away from something like Pather Panchali . The other thing to mention is the rather avant-garde sound design, which at times felt like something from a surrealist film, in particular the use of non-diegetic sound effects to portray Neeta’s state of mind.  It’s a matter of taste, but personally I found the sound design rather distracting and distancing, especially within a setting which otherwise emphasises realism. So overall, I was disappointed and, by its end, more than a little bored with The Cloud-Capped Star .  I can see from other reviews on here that the film gets a lot of love and I wish I could share in that, but sadly it just did not work for me.

All the pieces are here for a film I should love. It is beautifully shot, with great use of close-ups and intricate camera moves. It is gorgeous to look at. It's a story about a young woman in India during the Partition of India, where her poor family are trying to carve out a life for themselves. Unfortunately for this woman her family takes advantage of her. She takes on all the responsibility and continues to sacrifice herself for her ungrateful and uncaring family members, literally making herself sick to lift up those she cares about. All the while keeping silent and not condemning their actions. It has all the makings of a fantastic neorealist-esque social commentary and feminist film. Ghatak clearly has the technical mastery to put together a compelling, well shot movie. Why didn't this work for me? It may be the subtitles (on Amazon) were terrible. But more key is this movie really lays into the melodrama, and for me the line between great melodrama and an absolute slog is very thin. It is overly maudlin and gets repetitive, only broken by long interludes of music that don't help the pacing. On paper I love this movie, in practice it didn't move me. Family melodrama about a young woman who continually sacrifices everything for her ungrateful family and gets nothing in return, sort of like a reverse Tokyo Story , minus the subtlety and the dignity. Beautifully shot, to be sure (especially the first two shots, opening with Neeta, the protagonist, walking in front of an impossibly beautiful and massive tree followed by a split diopter shot of Neeta in the foreground, her singing brother in the middle ground and a moving train in the background, all in focus), but rather poorly edited and even more poorly acted. Gita Ghatak as Neeta's younger sister is especially bad and also looks too old to be playing her younger sister (I looked them up, and she was in fact four years older than Supriya Choudhury, who plays Neeta). The melodrama comes almost to the brink of self-parody, so that you pretty much know what 's going to happen beat for beat if you've ever seen any melodrama in your life ("This was expected," says the father when his youngest son has an accident at the factory where he works ... yes, it was). It also uses weird sound effects to denote Neeta's emotional state in case you couldn't tell by her overacting.

Director- Ritwik Ghatak. This is the first film I have seen of his. The first thing I faced while watching this film was comparing it with other films of the year that were released in the world. However, doing that is a folly, as India, unlike other countries, didn't have a dedicated Cinematic Canon before the generation of Satyajit Ray, Bimal Roy, Ritwik Ghatak, etc. Or so is my opinion, as I have watched seldom of India before the 60s. The music of the film is a highlight for me, and I also appreciated the way the shots were framed. The premise reminded me of Rocco and his Brothers, and I found this film to be a lot better than it because of my hatred for this type of martyrdom. Meghe Dhaka Tara has no clear antagonist, except maybe the intellect of the protagonist for the most part. I chuckled every time she made another dumb decision of self-sacrifice, and then felt sad or cried about it. Folks might watch the film and consider the sister to be evil, but I just find her opportunistic and not a complete narcissist, as she so said that Sanat, the protagonist's boyfriend, has his limits too. Why would he wile away his life waiting for a person who so vehemently tries to lie on the ground and be trampled by others? This time around, I saw it to be much more on the side of anti-martyrdom due to some sequences in the second half. Particularly, the ending where she screams repeatedly, "I want to live". I also liked some scenes where the protagonist talks back at those who have made it their life's mission to screw her over after drying her of everything she has, including her soul and will to live. I liked how the oldest freeloader sibling got verbally thrashed by the younger brother and the shopkeeper. The family indeed mostly comprised of beggars, with the oldest sibling being the main one. He indeed turns his life around later on, but it was too late as the protagonist succumbed to the pressure that was not only loaded on her but which she took enthusiastically. After a point, it indeed felt like this is another run-of-the-mill Pro Martyrdom Selfless Woman suffering for the whole of the runtime slop, as I so believed during my first watch, which made me hate it. But some aspects that offer a more meta view made me look more favorably towards it. I loved the ending where the shopkeeper tells the oldest brother that the family, now living in their second-story house, has completely forgotten the protagonist, because of which their financial progress could happen. This is the fate deserving of those who are dumb enough to fall for such martyrdom. The way she chose a slow and painful process of dying from TB, if not for the oldest brother finding it out, shows us that even after all this time, she really did find pleasure in her dumb behaviour. Her suffering from TB could be considered as a meta commentary too, as TB affected her breathing, and she indeed felt suffocated with her family. One could even view this film through the lens of Giri, responsibility and Ninjo, human desire, where Giri, which dominated her whole life, is the cause of her suffering. She never pursued her Ninjo, and hence her life was devoid of any joy whatsoever. What I really liked about the film is that Ghatak never sensationalises her plight, instead choosing to show the situation as it is. I can see how this would have been groundbreaking for its time but it doesn't age as well as some other films of that era. Such as Waqt, Pyaasa, Kaagaz ke Phool, Awara, Chalti ka naam Gaadi, etc. Overall, a good film, but not something I see myself ever revisiting in the future for the third time.

In The Cloud-Capped Star , director Ritwik Ghatak is interested in how larger social-economic backgrounds impact the daily personal lives and social intimacies of the average person. The life of the individual acts as the catalyst towards these large-scale industrial changes underlying society. The rapid motion of the train in one of the earliest sequences of the film, which travels in the direction of Neeta (the protagonist), mirrors the rapid advancements that industrialization (a catalyst from India’s newfound independence given the context this film was released in) act as a means of rapidly changing the dynamics of the characters’ lives (if only present in the background). The use of music and general sound design functions as an on-the-nose connection between how the characters feel, especially on the metaphorical or metaphysical level. Juxtaposing their personal familial struggles to that of the mythical lyrics of the songs creates the notion that musical numbers function in two contrasting, yet complimentary ways. On the one hand, they harm the overall sense of realism that the film exhibits, but at the same time also work to express the repressed emotional sentiments of the interpersonal relationships of the film's characters that could not otherwise be depicted without music. The aesthetic close-up shots are very prominent, especially in the melodrama which of course allows for the intrigue of personal depth and insight into the emotions of the characters in this film, especially in the scene where Neeta and her brother sing together. This reflects an earlier scene in which Neeta is asked if her and her brother will be singing together, prompting her to say that she gave it up. We later see in the scene where they sing together in the dark room that she is only able to sing in these moments of intimacy and overall personal time. The presence of her brother then, indicates a closeness that she only shares with him as opposed to the rest of her family. Melodrama also functions as a political critique as it focuses on these internal struggles of family that are exacerbated by the advent of rapid industrialization around them.  Melodrama seems to exist in these extreme opposites of who is good and who is bad, but there also exists the historical contradictions within the film. For instance, her father recognizes all the ways in which Neeta is being exploited, but is inevitably the one to kick her out.  This creates a contrast to her internal struggles and the context she exists in. In this way, the film also bears similarities to the Italian Neo-realism film movement, but also cranks the realism up to a heightened level that can only be found in melodrama. Given this understanding we can look back to the train and understand it as a creation with the propensity to bring about Sysiphian repercussions. The train may represent progress, but the fact that the people keep repeating or perpetuating their condition, whether it be asking for donation money or treating Neeta poorly demonstrates that progress must come from both the individuals and society.

THE CLOUD-CAPPED STAR is an Indian melodrama from 1960, filmed in gorgeous black and white.  It's an interesting story about the long-suffering eldest daughter in a formerly genteel Hindu family that has been displaced by the Partition in 1947.  In this family education and "white-collar" employment had been taken for granted, but they are now in a small house in what is basically a refugee camp.  The eldest daughter, Nita, makes some money tutoring, and seems to be the main (or even only) bread-winner.  She is stoic and dutiful to a fault, and spends nothing on herself so her family can scrape by and keep up appearances. Nita reminded me somewhat of George Bailey from IT'S A WONDERFUL LIFE or even Eleanor Dashwood from "Sense and Sensibility."  Except there's no guarantee that things will turn out for the best, or even that Nita's family will be grateful.  CLOUD-CAPPED STAR explores the idea that letting people walk all over you may not do them or you any good. I love that idea, but the style of this movie kept me from loving it on the whole.  It is melodramatic in style as well as substance, and some of the flamboyant, on-the-nose dialog and music detracted from my enjoyment.  There were also many instances where I could tell from the dramatic scoring that something significant had happened, but I didn't have the cultural or historical understanding to know what.  But obviously the way a certain person was dressed in one scene (for instance) was a big deal for some reason, and in another scene a character laughed and smiled at what seemed like a jarringly inappropriate moment.  I'm sure the intended audience would know what was going on, but I was sometimes at a loss.  I didn't even know the importance of the Partition to these characters--I found that out from Wikipedia. I liked this film, and it was certainly interesting throughout, but I was never involved enough emotionally for me to call it great.

"The sheer poignancy pulsating through The Cloud-Capped Star should not be underestimated, since so much of what makes this such a powerful film resides in these moments of almost ethereal meandering, whereby Ghatak is commenting on some complex themes through the guise of a poetic narrative that touches on so many resonant ideas. Combining heartfelt melodrama with sequences of magical realism (such as the sporadic moments where we see Shankar walking through the countryside singing, which gives the film a necessary boost of energy, and allows its progress to be noted through his growing confidence in his skills, one of the many small nuances Ghatak infuses into the film) was a challenging task, but the director does so beautifully, finding the truth in a very difficult story. Yet, what lingers the most about The Cloud-Capped Star isn’t the mechanics of its plot, or the various strands of dialogue that carry a great deal of meaning, but rather the emotions evoked throughout it. Despite the bleak nature of the story, Ghatak composes an exceptionally hopeful film – this film would not have been nearly as meaningful had it not carried some sense of impossible optimism, and even when it is spiralling towards complete despair, there is some feeling of hope. Inarguably, this film doesn’t have a traditionally happy ending – if anything, the climax is the most haunting aspect of the entire film. However, if we strip away the ambiguities accompanied with the ending, and instead look at what message it conveys – that of defeating the odds and surviving by any means possible – we can easily understand why this is such a profoundly effective work of cinematic realism. Ghatak truly made nothing short of a masterpiece with The Cloud-Capped Star, a powerful and heart-wrenchingly beautiful social drama that finds the hope in the most impossible of situations." moviesunchained.wordpress.com/2020/10/22/the-cloud-capped-star-1960/

The delicately observed interactions and trials of an impoverished intellectual family (Hindu refugees on the outskirts of Calcutta fleeing post-Partition Pakistan, though I wouldn't have figured this out from the movie if I hadn't known it already).  Starts out in a slightly poetic, slightly exaggerated social realist vein reminiscent of Renoir, with the English-obsessed father's comic relief and the mother always about to blow a gasket.  As it progresses it takes a hard turn into melodrama, with an escalating series of tragedies that hit one daughter, the excessively selfless protagonist, the hardest.  The performances and direction are an odd mix of naturalism and overemphasis, with the music cues to denote psychological states and reactions especially a bit much.  I find this kind of stylistic lane-jumping takes me out of the action, particularly in any scenes involving the lead's asshole boyfriend.  Overall I do like Ghatak's fundamentally humanist style, which mostly eschews establishing or traveling shots to focus on the characters, with the exception of the wider, usually palate-cleansing shots of the road from school to the family's home, and a more impressionistic sequence in the countryside toward the end. 'The Cloud-Capped Star' is about Nita, who has to take care of her middle-class family when her father has an accident and can no longer earn a living. No one, not even her mother, sister, or older brother, wants to take on the role of the breadwinner of the family, so the burden falls on the loyal, responsible Nita. 'The Cloud-Capped Star' is the second installment in director Ritwik Ghatak’s partition trilogy. Nita and her family are refugees from East Pakistan, and Nita is a “cloud-capped star”: her potential is dimmed by the clouds and the dark night. Ghatak’s film places great emphasis on the characters’ inner experiences through surrealistic use of music and beautiful framing. It’s clear that Ghatak invested a great deal of time in conveying his vision, but the music and sound effects do feel a bit excessive at times. The story was also a little predictable. And while the framing of the cinematography was generally beautiful, the execution was sometimes a bit amateurish (as in: some rare shots weren’t in focus). What I did found interesting was that the film has a more lighthearted, ‘comedic’ side; there are playful moments, and there’s a certain sentimentality to the characters. This is especially evident in Nita’s relationship with her brother, as both characters clearly have dreams. Within this framework, the portrayal of the father fell flat, as the actors portrayal borders on caricature. But otherwise, this tone ensured that the film didn’t become an overemphasized victim story. I did like 'The Cloud-Capped Star' a lot, despite my criticisms. Specifically because of the clear choices made: the tone, the music, and the framing. The ending puts a clear exclamation mark behind the message. All over the world, there are "cloud-capped stars". Women with so much potential, who are overshadowed by the care they must provide and by the course of history. Their story is embedded into the story of their family, which is embedded into historical shifts. Ghatak manages to seamlessly connect an individual’s story to the systematic struggle and the bigger picture.

Ritwik Ghatak’s Indian cinema The Cloud-Capped Star (Meghe Dhaka Tara) delivers a harrowing portrait of displacement and human greed through the tragic unraveling of Nita, a self-sacrificing young woman supporting her refugee family in post-partition Bengal. Set against the backdrop of a fractured homeland where survival overrides morality, the film employs stark symbolism, such as Nita's fatal tuberculosis representing the parasitic consumption of her spirit by an ungrateful family, and a recurring whipping sound effect that echoes her emotional trauma. Ghatak masterfully contrasts the suffocating confines of the family's refugee tenement with the vast, indifferent majesty of nature, a motif that peaks in the film's most iconic scenes. From the ominous opening setup featuring Pandit Ravi Shankar’s piercing sitar score to the heartbreaking moment Nita is quietly abandoned by her fiancé Sanat for her own sister, the narrative builds toward one of cinema's most devastating climaxes. On a hillside facing the open horizon, Nita lets out a final, agonizing cry, "Brother, I want to live!", cementing her status as the ultimate emotional and financial anchor destroyed by the very people she sought to save.

Nita never remained just a character to me. Gradually, she began to feel like a reflection of all those people who keep silencing their own desires, one after another, simply to keep their families afloat. Everyone takes something from her—her time, her labor, her affection, her sacrifices. Yet so few ever stop to ask what, if anything, is left for Nita herself. Ritwik Ghatak never attempts to make emotion look beautiful. At times, he leaves it so raw that certain scenes become almost uncomfortable to watch. And that discomfort is precisely where the film draws much of its power. A sudden sound, a fleeting expression, an abrupt cut—everything seems to externalize the pressure building inside the characters. While watching, I often felt that I wasn't witnessing a story at all; I was watching a family slowly consume one of its own. The film's visual language carries that same sense of anguish. The interplay of light and shadow, the mountains, the dilapidated surroundings, and the claustrophobic spaces gradually make Nita's world feel as though it is shrinking along with her. Some frames are so emotionally charged that they remain in memory not as images, but as sensations. And Supriya Devi's portrayal of Nita—calling it simply "extraordinary" almost feels inadequate. The exhaustion in her eyes, the restrained resentment on her face, and that fragile strength in her voice, always hovering just before it breaks, never feel like a performance. It feels as though we are witnessing a real human life quietly coming apart in front of us. Perhaps the most heartbreaking thing about Nita is that she never asks for anything extraordinary. She only longs for a little affection, a little peace, and the smallest space in which to live on her own terms. Maybe that is why Meghe Dhaka Tara still feels so painfully relevant after all these years. Time has changed, cities have changed, and the way we live has changed—but people who place everyone's needs before their own are still everywhere. And perhaps the tragedy is that we continue to notice what they give us far more easily than we notice what their giving has taken away from them.

The Criterion Challenge 2026 Progress: 29/52 Category: Glorious Restorations My first Ritwik Ghatak film, and it's strange that, despite being Indian, I only came to know about him through the Criterion Collection. It says a lot about how little recognition many of India's greatest filmmakers receive in their own country. Alongside Satyajit Ray 's work, Meghe Dhaka Tara is a reminder of how extraordinary Bengali cinema was at a time when mainstream Bollywood was largely churning out broad entertainment for the masses—a trend that, in many ways, continues today. On the surface, this is a sentimental and often melodramatic film, but beneath that lies a remarkably nuanced portrayal of social reality, poverty, and the role of women in post-Independence Bengal. Ghatak's neorealist approach immerses you completely in its world. The story follows Nita, the self-sacrificing eldest daughter of a refugee family, who shoulders the burden of supporting everyone around her while gradually watching her own dreams, relationships, and health slip away. There are no true villains here—only ordinary people shaped by desperation and circumstance. The central conflict between personal ambition and familial responsibility is deeply affecting, and the tragic injustice of Nita's exploitation by those closest to her is portrayed with heartbreaking honesty. The plot itself is simple and predictable, with few surprises, but Ghatak's direction and the performances keep it engaging throughout. I did feel the pacing could have been tighter, and the heightened melodrama occasionally felt a bit too much. Still, the emotional core remains powerful. Supriya Choudhury completely stole the show. Her performance is wonderfully restrained when it needs to be, yet she never hesitates to be emotionally expressive during the film's devastating moments. Her performance in her final scene is especially heartbreaking. Her character reminded me a great deal of Setsuko Hara in Ozu' s Late Spring —both women postpone their own happiness out of a sense of duty toward their dependent families. Good visuals. Ghatak fills every frame with thoughtful compositions, often using depth of field to keep certain characters out of focus for heightened emotional effect. His use of surreal, almost jarring sound design at key moments is quite effective. I noticed some similarities with Satyajit Ray's Apu Trilogy. One interesting similarity is how both filmmakers populate their worlds with characters deeply connected to art and music. Perhaps it reflects the intellectual and cultural climate of Bengal at the time, where artistic pursuits held a special place in society. If you're a fan of Satyajit Ray, this is an easy recommendation. It's not flawless, but it's a deeply moving film whose emotional and social observations linger long after the credits roll. The climax of meghe Dhaka Tara felt like the emotional eruption of everything the film and Neeta had suppressed and endured. What’s extraordinary is that the film never directly explains the historical trauma shaping its world. Nobody sits down and talks about Partition explicitly yet it’s present in everything like the financial ruin, the emotional decay, the refugee settlement, the collapse of the traditional Bengali middle class family structure. Ritwik Ghatak embeds history into the atmosphere itself naturally. The sound design by Ghatak was extraordinary. Ghatak doesn’t use sound naturally but rather psychologically. The sudden industrial noises, train sounds and the recurring whip like cracks feel like emotional ruptures breaking into ordinary life. Whenever tenderness or hope begins to emerge, reality violently intrudes through sound. The soundtrack becomes the nervous system of the film, expressing trauma that the characters themselves cannot express. Music is equally central to the film’s meaning. This is most powerfully embodied through Shankar. While the family struggles to survive, he dedicates himself to music, appearing detached and impractical. But Ghatak never mocks him because he sees art as spiritually necessary even in poverty. Shankar’s eventual success as a musician becomes deeply painful because it exists at the cost of Neeta’s gradual destruction. That’s the film’s cruel brilliance. Shankar’s freedom to pursue art is only possible because Neeta silently sacrifices everything for the family. She supports everyone emotionally and financially while slowly losing her own future, health and desires. The film never presents this as simple villainy because nobody consciously decided to exploit her. What makes Shankar tragic too is that he may be the only person who truly understands Neeta’s suffering. Because he is an artist and he possesses emotional sensitivity that others lack. Ghatak creates a devastating contradiction where the least economically useful person becomes the most emotionally aware.

I watched this without subtitles, which didn't seriously impede my understanding but was not ideal for understanding every single word. (Something interesting about a movie in a language you don't quite have mastery over is that the dialogue seems quieter because your brain has a harder time recognizing words and separating them from the ambient noise.) What it did do, though, is prime me to pay especially close attention to the language. To varying extents, all the men in the movie mix English words into their Bengali, while the women do not except when explicitly echoing a man. The foreign viewer is inclined to think of English as the language of modernity and advancement and the native language as connected to the traditional past, but the associations are different here: English is the language of dreamers and intellectuals, of would-be gentlemen putting on airs and of second-class degrees in pure physics that lead to nothing, while Bengali is the language of people who have to work for a living. The one scene set in an anglophone environment is the one scene completely removed from the material concerns of life in Calcutta. The classic stereotype of the Bengali is as an ineffectual intellectual. This archetype is most obviously represented here by the invalid father who sits and quotes Wordsworth while his education does nothing to provide for his family. It's tempting to take this story of a family fallen on hard times as a metaphor for the decline of Bengal from the richest province in India to its present state, a process that would have already been evident in 1960.

The sound design is incredible — those sudden, almost violent bursts of sound make the film feel like Nita’s inner world is breaking apart in real time. Melodramatic, haunting and devastating without ever feeling cheap. A film about a woman who gives everyone a life, while quietly losing her own.

삶에서 죽음으로, 횡에서 종으로. 고전적 대가들이 화면을 구성할 때 우리는 미학으로서가 아니라 연극적 의미에서 미장센을 확인할 수 있다. 오프닝 속 두 번째 쇼트 부터 리트윅 가탁은 이를 직접적으로 보여준다. 저 멀리 거대한 나무 사이로 한 여성이 다가오며 이내 그녀는 이후 오빠로 밝혀지는 남성을 바라본다. 그리고 우리는 그 사이로 후경 속 기차가 수평의 운동을 하는 것을 목격할 수 있다. 물론 이러한 방식 자체는 미조구치나 샤오시엔, 특히나 포드나 르누아르 등 많은 이들에 의해 사용되고는 한 것이다. 허나 여기서 우리가 주목해야 할 점은 고전적 영화가 가장 많이 빚을 지고 있는 연극에서 비롯된 미장센이 줄곧 수평의 측면에서만 이루어졌다는 점이다. 이는 중력이라는 행성의 한계 때문이기도 하다. 극에서 무대 오른쪽에서 왼쪽으로 그 반대로 이동하는 이들의 모습이 그렇듯 <구름에 가린 별> 속 창문, 스크린 등 프레임 사이로 바라봐지는 이들의 움직임은 수평의 운동으로 존재한다. 그렇기에 인류가 죽음을 승천, 연기와 같이 수평이 아닌 수직의 운동으로 생각했음은 중력이라는 삶의 한계에서 벗어난 상태라는 상상 때문에 가능한 것 아닌가도 싶다. 적어도 영화에서 추락과 상승은 모티브 이상이 되지 못하는 이유 또한 거기에 있다. 수평 운동의 경우 피사체를 직접 따라갈 수 있지만 수직 운동의 경우 애초에 추락이 수 초 단위로 끝나는데다가 카메라의 파손이라는 물리적 한계를 맞이하기 때문이다. 이 영화 속 기차는 계속해서 삶의 역경 사이를 파고 든다. 주인공 니타가 가정 형편 때문에 사낫과 결혼하지 못하고 기다림을 약속하는 장면을 생각해보자. 오프닝과 같이 저 멀리 기차는 프레임에 침입하여 횡의 움직임, 삶이라는 한계를 드러낸다. 여기서 리트윅 가탁이 훌륭한 점은 이윽고 드러나는 죽음을 곧바로 종의 상태로 드러낸다는 점이다. 바로 다음 쇼트 속, 니타의 아버지는 기찻길을 걷다 쓰러지며 일할 수 있는 상태가 아님이 드러난다. 이 장면에서 이전 수평으로 놓여져 있던 철도는 사선으로 변하며 아버지의 몸 상태를 확인 한 니타는 로우 앵글 속 수직의 나선 계단을 일일이 내려오는 모습을 보여준다. 횡의 운동이 종의 운동으로 변한 것이다. 이후 리트윅 가탁은 수직으로 내리는 비, 가마솥의 연기 등으로 종의 운동을 지속적으로 드러내며 그 때 마다 주인공 니타는 희생 속에서 점점 곪아가며 죽음에 이르게 된다. 수많은 평론가들이 지적하듯 멜로 영화에 가학적 성향이 존재하기는 하지만 이 정도로 직접적으로 고통을 보여주지 않고 참혹함을 드러내는 영화 또한 몇 없다고 여기는데 정작 오빠인 샤카가 성공하여 폐렴에 걸린 니타를 병원에 입원시키는 시퀀스를 생각해보자. 이 때 리트윅 가탁은 산 위의 구름에서 점차 산 중턱, 아래, 그리고는 결국 그들이 살던 마을로 카메라를 이동하며 하강의 상태를 통해 이전과 다를 바 없는 죽음을 드러내고 있다. 결국 그렇기에 니타의 마지막 울부짖음 "난 살고 말거야!"는 그녀의 사형 선고나 다름 없으리라. 여기서 니타의 파국의 전조가 오로지 시선으로 드러남을 이야기해야만 할 테다. 약혼자인 사낫과 함께 있을 때 마다 걱정스러운 듯 그들을 바라보는 어머니와 먹이를 노리듯 사낫을 바라보는 동생 지타의 시선들, 이는 니타가 시집 가면 더 이상 집안의 돈을 벌어올 수 없는 상태에 대한 두려움과 언니의 약혼자를 가로채 신분 상승의 욕망을 취하려는 이의 시선이다. 작중 지속적으로 180도 선을 어기는 시선 쇼트 속 지타의 시선이 사낫과 맞았음을 상기하게 된다. 헌데 아이러니하게도 이러한 시선은 니타에게도 존재한다. 계속해서 창 밖을 바라보며 어딘가를 바라보는 모습, 이상을 추구하며 현실에 안주하지 않는 이의 모습은 역설적으로 현실에 저항하지 못하는 이의 초상으로 변화한다. 니타 자신이 말하듯 그녀의 죄는 현실을 거부하지 못한 죄이다. 그렇기에 그녀의 처지를 바라볼 수 밖에 없던 아버지는 그녀를 놓아주기 위해 내쫓듯 하지 않았던가? 창 밖을 바라보던 여성이 창 밖으로 나가게 된 순간, 하지만 이 순간 마저도 오빠에 의해 저지 되며 그녀는 병원으로 들어가게 된다. 여기서 프레임이란 일찍이 르누아르가 보여주었듯 극과 현실, 무대와 객석 등의 경계이다. 하지만 그 사이로 바라보며 이상을 꿈꾸던 니타는 결국 경계를 넘나들지 못하며 극은 종결된다. 그럼에도 우리는 그녀가 떠나려던 순간 내리는 비의 수직 운동이 얼마나 역동적이었는지를 기억해야 할 테다. 누군가 죽어도 삶은 계속되며 삶은 종종 죽음을 망각한다. 니타를 병문안 간 오빠의 시퀀스 속 이전과 같이 기차의 경적 소리가 울리지만 우리는 결코 화면에서 기차를 발견할 수 없다. 마을로 금의환향한 오빠 샹카가 자신의 동생과 처지가 비슷해 보이는 여성을 발견하며 망연자실 할 수 밖에 없던 이유 또한 마찬가지이다. 인간은 태생적 한계로 인해 단 한 번의 종의 운동(죽음)을 실행할 수 있지만 그 이전까지는 어떻게든 횡의 운동(삶)을 이어가야만 한다. 마르크스주의의 미학을 이어받은 이들 중 개인적으로 구조 영화 감독들 보다 극영화를 찍은 이들이 가지고 있는 이점이 바로 여기에 있다고 여긴다. 극이라는 엄밀함, 기호들은 인간에 의해 감춰지기에 그 사이의 상호작용을 할 수 있다. 고전 할리우드 감독들의 연출이 소련의 몽타주 학파와는 달리 연출을 감추는 엄밀함 속에 존재하며 그저 스토리를 전달하려 했음을 다시 한 번 떠올리게 된다. 하스미 시게히코의 지적 처럼 여기서 역전이 일어나게 된다. 이미지를 직접적으로 전달하려던 이들의 영화는 반대로 상상을 불가케 하며 이미지를 수단으로 사용하려던 이들의 영화는 그 사이의 교류, 상상을 가능케 한다. 나는 후자의 방식을 선호한다. 이미지는 초월로 이끄는 하나의 도구일 뿐이라 여기기 때문이다.

Everything about this movie is great. But if I had to single out what struck me the most, it would be the cinematic composition. Ritwik Ghatak makes use of a wide array of techniques, and each one serves to frame the scene in a meaningful way regarding the drama that is unfolding, the psychological state of a character, a mood… I found especially beautiful the wide-angle shots of landscapes and nature. There is one that happens more than once where two characters are sitting next to a river. They are filmed from the road and every now and then someone passes and stops to look at them. This switches the couple to the middle ground, and the observer becomes the foreground of the image. Then, suddenly, a train crosses the very background adding even more depth of field; everything is in focus. And this is just one example, almost every shot is a painting in Meghe Dhaka Tara . There is a lot of interesting symbolism in the film too. The trains that, whilst in Anna Karenina bring modernity and freedom, in here break the tranquillity and peace of the natural scenery. An intellectual father who can only quote English poets while his good-for-nothing son sings Tagore. A sound design full of effects like buzzing, high pitched notes or the crack of whips interspaced with bewitching traditional music. In several instances Nita is filmed through window shutters and bars conveying oppression, there are also angles that frame the head as if choking the character… This is definitely a film to be studied and, with my poor knowledge of Indian history, particularly the partition times, I can barely scratch the surface. Ritwik Ghatak is a brilliant director who needs to be talked about much more in the west, I hope I can continue watching his filmography and learning from his cinema.

Neeta è l’unica fonte di reddito in famiglia. Il fratello chiede sempre soldi in prestito col sogno d’affermarsi come cantante, mentre il fidanzato, laureatosi ingegnere, non riesce a trovare un lavoro all’altezza delle proprie competenze. Anima gentile e predisposta al sacrificio, la ragazza attende con fiducia un futuro migliore. Dopo A River called Titas, una vetta del cinema di Ghatak. L'intensità del melodramma e la necessità della denuncia sociale, binomio presente in gran parte dei suoi film, vanno qui più che mai di pari passo alla consueta ricchezza di invenzioni visive e sonore. La regione del Bengala è un personaggio aggiunto, coi suoi corsi d’acqua e i suoi alberi rigogliosi, simboli di vita in contrasto coi problemi economici che affliggono i protagonisti, avvicinandoli a uno stato di morte, effettiva o apparente. Il dialogo tra le figure umane e gli ambienti è mediato da una colonna sonora regolata da canti e percussioni, termometro di una voglia di vivere che verrà urlata nel momento più struggente del film. Il crescendo finale è elevato da uno stile febbrile che fa spiccare il volo alle possibilità della macchina da presa, restituendo vertiginosamente il tormento e l’estasi del racconto.

This intimate (those close-ups!) and suffocating film depicts the life of a refugee family following the Partition of Bengal, although the political context sits very much in the background. There are shades of Ozu in this illustration of poverty and family life, with the elder daughter sacrificing her dreams to help her siblings achieve theirs whilst also being “the breadwinner”. It’s a melodrama of the highest order, with some of the most harrowing use of music in all cinema; Shankar’s songs are his route to riches, but they also provide an ironic counterpoint to the film’s gut punch of an ending.

This is probably director Ritwik Ghatak's most celebrated film, and watching it for the first time, it feels as if it's for good reasons. If his debut film had a sort of hazy poetic realism, this one leads harder into melodrama. Nothing ever feels forced or unnatural but the compositions are very carefully arranged, with characters rarely looking at one another. The depth of field is brought into play with all kinds of wonderfully elegant, and moving, shots of characters viewing others from afar with empathy and sadness. The primary tragedy in the film is for the eldest daughter Neeta, who forgoes a lot of her own desires to help her family and support those around her (a classic melodramatic plot), and things get progressively tougher for her, though the film never lets that more melancholy register overwhelm the delicate balance of individual stories. Ghatak also pushes some of the other formal qualities, such as the sound design: while the gloomy setting and monochrome cinematography may suggest the realism he started with, this is far more expressionist than is initially apparent, every bit as staged as a Sirk film in some ways, though the performances are more carefully reined in and the emotions largely turned inwards. Anyway, I need to see it again; this is wonderful stuff.

Even more interestingly, her brother Shankar almost seems to hear it in the scene where he checks himself before he too forsakes the path she sacrificed her youth to set him on. The point of all this aural expressionism is perhaps best exemplified by one of the film's outstanding visual moments, a rack focus to a Falconetti close-up of Neeta's face in the foreground when she finally castigates her mother for taking her for granted. The Passion of Joan of Arc is about the trial and tribulations of a saint about to ascend to heaven; Star is set in the hell that is other people.

Life is nothing but a waterfall cascading through uneven steps, meandering intricately at places. Each one of us has something to offer, love– maddening love is one of them. Each one of us has a spark, so specifically ours. Some of us want to protect it, some lose it halfway adapting to the normalcy of life and expectations. But there are some who are eager to lose that spark only because they want that very spark to light up the darkness their loved ones are in. Even if that means the glaze from their skin will wear off, gone will be the desires of their own and all they would be left with is a heart grieving for the life that could've been theirs. Eyes that craved dreams and embroidered them with illuminating stars would be left awake in the whole black of the night until the skin beside them turns brown. But it's very disheartening to know the people they can give up everything for want them only because of the effort they give; that they are not needed once the convenience that comes with their presence is not there. Maybe we think we can go on with everything, that it's okay to not speak up sometimes, that perhaps we can try and get over it. But sometimes all we need to do is to speak. To let the words that have been at the rim of our lips fall. Perhaps to stay hidden like a capped star is an art but sometimes it's a curse too. Because once in a while even the hidden star hopes for the clouds to step aside. Once in a while it too wants to shine. But they think they can go without it— happiness. And once they come to realize, it's too late. All they can say then is — “I wanted to live, all I wanted was to live.” And soon they turn into ash and the spark is extinguished once and for all. And what is the need to be hidden if you are not there at all? So speak when your heart and mind battle. Perhaps it really is better to speak than to die. One of the great melodramas of dislocation and displacement. Neeta (Supriya Choudhury) is a young woman whose labour, patience and self-sacrifice form the only glue holding together a declassé Bengali family uprooted from East Bengal after Partition. But Ghatak continually expands her suffering beyond the private sphere. Rather than some naive victim, Neeta is at once a fully fleshed-out character, all the more believable in her pain for having the intelligence, wit and wherewithal to realise she is throwing her life away for people who don't deserve it, as well as a stand-in for countless other refugees of Partition. This is clear by the final shot, when the film suggests another young woman might be another Neeta. Melodrama as always with Ghatak thus becomes the vehicle through which a collective historical trauma can be emotionally expressed and reflected for the mass audience who have lived through it. But Ghatak also fractures melodrama conventions by adding a wide range of audiovisual influences and techniques: Bengali folk and devotional music, Tagore song, theatrical gesture, Soviet montage, expressionist lighting and camera angles, violently modernist sound (the famous cracks, whiplashes, and other non-diegetic noises on the soundtrack which seem almost to make the deep fissure of Bengal itself audible). Visually, trains, fences, lattices and makeshift structures cut across rivers, trees, hills and open landscapes, setting arbitrary man-made lines against images of organic rootedness and a lost homeland --- the latter having been divided by the former through Partition. When I first watched, Neeta's famous cry reminded me a bit of that ending in Tsai Ming-liang's Vive L'Amour, another moment of raw emotion which, taken out of context, might seem too much, but which through the accumulation of the film up to that point builds up into a devastating and universal expression of existential anguish. Now, on second viewing it feels so clear Neeta is carrying something more, the weight of the history of an entire people and nation.
A visual poem by Ghatak about a tragic tale. The sound design will stay with me forever. I don't know if it's recency bias, but I don't think I've seen a better Bengali film than this yet.

I don't have the words but I'm going to try anyway. There are films you watch, There are films you remember and then there are films that just settle somewhere deep inside you and never leave. Meghe Dhaka Tara is the third kind. This film has made its place in my top 4 permanently. This man made only eight feature films in his entire life and he died at just fifty years old, never having found the wide audience he deserved. Meghe Dhaka Tara is actually the first part of what people now call his Partition Trilogy, the other two being Komal Gandhar and Subarnarekha. All three films deal with the pain of Bengal's partition, a wound that stayed with ghatak his whole life because he himself lived through it. He was not making films about something he read about. He was making films about something that broke him personally and you can feel that in every single frame of this movie. The tragedy is that most of his films were either ignored or never even properly released while he was alive. infact his very first film was never released in his lifetime, Nagarik, the first film ghatak ever made, was completed in 1953 but released in 1977, a year after he died. The world only started truly appreciating him after he was gone. That is one of the saddest things I know about cinema. I have watched this twice now, i cried both times. Multiple times. I am not going to tell you exactly which moments made me cry because honestly i think if you watch this film with an open heart, you will find your own moments and they will break you in your own way. I need to say something about myself before i talk about this film, because i think it matters. When i watch a film like this, something deep, intense, emotionally heavy. I don't just observe it from outside. I fall into it completely. I stop being a person watching characters and I just start living alongside them. With other kinds of films I  can sit back and enjoy normally. But with a film like this one, that is impossible for me. I dissolve into it entirely. I feel what they feel. Their world becomes my world. That is how I watched Nita, i was not looking at her from a distance, i was right there with her in those small tight rooms, feeling the weight of everything she was carrying, watching the people around her take from her again and again without even stopping to notice what it was costing her. That is why this film hit me as hard as it did. Because i was not watching someone suffer. I was there. Nita- What Ghatak does with this character is something i have rarely seen in a film from any country. Nita is not dramatic about her pain. She does not ask for sympathy. She just keeps going. She smiles when she should be screaming. She adjusts when she should be walking away. She holds her entire family together with her bare hands and nobody around her thinks to ask how she is doing. Not because they are monsters, just because they are used to her being there. Used to her being strong. Used to her giving. And Supriya Choudhury plays her in a way that i genuinely do not have words for. She does not show you suffering like an actor performing suffering. She just is Nita. Every small movement, every look, every quiet moment where she says nothing but you can see everything going on inside her, it is one of the most real performances i have seen in my life. The moment when she understands what her own sister has done, there is no big dramatic scene. No shouting. Just a quiet realization that lands on her face like something heavy slowly settling and because she says nothing, because she does not fight back, because she just absorbs it, that is when you feel it the most because some kinds of hurt don't make you angry, They just make you go quiet and Nita goes very quiet. That one line on repeat "Dada, ami baachte chaai." I want to live. Both times i watched this film, this moment completely broke me and i mean that. Something in me just gave way when she said it. Because the entire film up to that point, Nita has been living for everyone else. Feeding everyone else. Sacrificing everything for everyone else and this one line is the first and only time she asks for something for herself, Just to live. Just that. And even that feels like too much to ask. No single line of dialogue has ever hit me the way this one did. Ghatak's craft- Ritwik Ghatak was doing things with this film in 1960 that still feel completely modern today and i want to talk about the technical side because I think it deserves more attention. The sound design in this film is extraordinary. It is not just background music to set a mood. It is layered and alive, you hear the world around the characters, the trains, the ambient noise of life continuing outside and then at certain emotional peaks, the sound suddenly bursts through in a way that feels like something internal breaking open. It is not a soundtrack telling you how to feel, it is sound being used as emotion itself. For 1960, this is extraordinary. Honestly even now it is extraordinary. And then there is the music. I need to talk about the music separately because it deserves its own space. There is a boat song in this film, "Majhi Tor Naam Janina" which roughly translates as "O boatman, i don't know your name, who will take me across the river? I have spent all my good days, and now I have come to the river." It is a traditional Bengali folk song, a Bhatiyali, the kind of song that boatmen on the rivers of Bengal used to sing but in this film it carries something much heavier than that because Ghatak himself was displaced by the Partition of Bengal. He lost his home. And these river songs, folk songs from the land he left behind feel like he is pouring his own grief directly into the film. And then there is Shankar. Nita's brother. At the beginning of the film he is a beginner singer. raw, unformed, still finding his voice. Throughout the film you hear him practising, growing, slowly becoming something. At one point Shankar sings a Rabindranath Tagore song, Je Raate Mor Duarguli, to Nita on her demand and after some time she starts singing along with him. Two siblings sitting together sharing a song, in the middle of everything falling apart around them. That moment of connection between them without any big dialogue or drama says more than words ever could. The song itself makes that moment even more painful if you know what it means. It is a Tagore song about a storm breaking open your doors in the middle of the night, everything going dark, reaching your arms out and finding nothing and not knowing that the storm itself was bringing something toward you. That is Nita's entire life described in one song. By the end of the film, when Shankar returns, he sings Lagi Lagan, and now he is a master. His voice has arrived completely. But here is what breaks you if you think about it. Who held the family together so Shankar could keep singing? Who sacrificed everything so he could have the space to grow? Nita. And by the time his voice becomes beautiful, she is gone. His rise and her fall happen in the same film, side by side, and Ghatak never underlines it or makes it obvious. He just shows you both things and lets you sit with what that means. And the framing. Ghatak keeps his shots tight and closed for almost the entire film. Small rooms, close faces, very little open space. You feel it physically, a kind of suffocation, a sense of being trapped. Which is exactly what Nita's life is. The frame itself is her life. There is one shot in this film that i cannot get out of my head which is also the poster of this film. Shankar has returned. He is famous now. The whole family is sitting outside in the courtyard, happy, celebrating and Nita is watching all of this from her room through a window made of iron bars. Ghatak does not show her full face, just her eyes. Two eyes looking through those iron bars at the family she gave everything to and those bars make her room look exactly like a prison cell. This woman who held that entire family together, who sacrificed her youth and her health and her love for every single one of them is now watching them be happy from behind that window. In her own home. That one shot says everything about what this film is about. No dialogue needed. No music needed. Just those two eyes behind bars. And then at the very end, the shot opens up. Suddenly there is sky. More sky than you have seen in the entire film. The first time i noticed this, on my second viewing, it stopped me completely. My first thought was freedom. She is finally released from everything she was carrying. But then i sat with it and i felt something more complicated than freedom. Because yes, she is free from her duties now but she has TB. She is alone. The family she gave everything to has moved on. So what kind of freedom is this? Is the sky opening up for her, or is it just that there is nothing left holding the frame together anymore? This is a hidden gem in the truest sense, When people talk about bengali/Indian cinema from this era, they talk about Satyajit Ray and Ray deserves everything he gets but Ritwik Ghatak was working at the same time, making films just as powerful, just as technically brilliant, just as emotionally devastating and most of the world still does not know his name. That is a real loss, not just for fans of Indian cinema but for anyone who cares about film as an art form. Meghe Dhaka Tara is not just a great film from its time and place. It is a extraordinary film. Full stop. It belongs in the conversation with the best cinema ever made anywhere in the world. This film does not push you toward an emotion. It does not tell you how to feel. It just places a life in front of you, ordinary, quiet, real and it trusts you enough to feel it yourself. This film will be the first name on my top four for the rest of my life. Not because i decided that because the film decided it for me. This made me feel something that i have never felt before. "Dada, ami baachte chaai."

It's founded on a very rigourous, scrupulous mise en scène , arranging actions with clear spatial geography, a series of comings-and-goings, people moving in and out of rooms—so perhaps like Lubitsch, or Sirk, etc. And for Ghatak, this means an immense freedom with his découpage , as if he could place the camera anywhere and maintain the film's integrity. The deftly composed deep-focus wide-angles shots, pushing forms into the lens barrel, become vertiginous simply by moving and cutting along the axis, and what would be "reverse shots" seem to open up these incredible, oblique counterpoints to the action. Ghatak moves very freely between the hieratic, the lyrical, and the natural.—And how do we even begin with the sound design!? One of those rare films where you feel the next shot can always surprise you; and  these "impossible" rapprochements of gaze and space always advance the film's melodrama, concentrating and distilling the emotions obliged by this violence. So this very self-sufficient, circuitous mise en scène is opened up in all directions while maintaining this form, like a kaleidoscope. Here's a little example, about forty-four minutes into the film: Nita and Sanat on a bench at a train station, at night, discussing their future; the first shot is a two-shot of them fairly head-on, both looking forwards; when she says they won't be getting married soon, he looks in her direction, cutting to the next shot with him in the foreground, the camera looking over his shoulders to see her at a slight diagonal; then when he's angered more, an incredible cut and movement—cutting on Sanat turning to look at Nita, we land on a closeup of him that, through a slight delay, follows his movement by panning to her in profile as she looks at him, before she effectively (and much more slowly) reciprocates the movements of both Sanat and the camera as she turns to look forwards, somewhere camera right; then the cut to a wide shot from behind, them small in the darkness, as they get up, walk around, and meet the panning camera in a very-striking two shot, a shaft of light cutting them at an angle, before, without cutting, Nita walks away again and the camera pans as she moves with the crowd into the background, Sanat left in the dark foreground. The cutting above, when broken down, is somewhat of an extreme extrapolation of shot-reverse shot, or some point-counterpoint, in how the angles complement and oppose one another. For the entirety of this sequence, the hard lighting is actually somewhat inconsistent, rather improbable, but without ever being so noticeable, the backlighting moving around with cuts, the shadows receiving them according to the dramatic movement. This estranges them from the somewhat crowded background, which falls into the night's darkness, until the scene's last composition "returning" Nita to that crowd. The sound design is a little quieter than expected of a public place, except when the bell rings. All these elements come together—the black-and-white photography, the setting, the quality of the night and the plasticity of the lighting—all depurate the dramatic scene and the melodramatic effect, as if the two were both very much part of this world but also the only people in the universe.

There is one scene, ONE scene, in this film that is its emotional centre. Before it, I thought that this is a good and thoughtful film but I felt like I was drifting through it. I was invested in the characters but not absolutely riveted by the story. After it, I felt very very changed. Like an realisation dawned on me that I could not have anticipated. This was the scene where Nita peers through the jaali at her whole family during their reunion, watching them reunite after having found their niches and accomplishing things they wanted to. She, in her dark room alone, like a kind of caged monster who no one wants anything to do with, after having given up all her ambitions and set aside her enormous talent for provide for those who leeched off of her shamelessly, is the sacrifice of Partition. She is the price that had to be paid for Bengal to overcome its losses. I wish I could capture what it felt to see just her eyes, watching through the jaali, closing and then opening, watching partly in envy, partly in love, and partly with a kind of fascination for the outside world that only someone who has gone mad can hold. But it’s impossible - and it’s impossible to really feel it by seeing the scene on its own; you have to watch the whole film to arrive at it and be struck by it. This is the scene the film rests on. After it, I had to sit up straight and my eyes burned the way I was locked on to the screen. I felt like I was watching an epic. That too, I felt like I was watching epic poetry. The story is so simple, revolving around a family whose eldest daughter Nita is the main breadwinner and has to give up on her academic pursuits to provide for the others, including her three siblings. Her siblings go on to find their own kinds of happiness. Her mother demeans her for all the reasons Indian mothers demean their daughters and her father, though sympathetic, ultimately goes mad, probably at seeing the unjust fate of his daughter and of all Bengal playing out in front of him. It doesn’t sound like much, and yet, in the course of the film, all of humanity’s pain is bundled up and thrown at you and, what, you are just meant to sit there in your seat and deal with it? I had to wait a while before writing a review because this film struck me so hard and so deep that I feel like I had to take a long breath before even beginning to unpack it in my mind. I remember learning about this whole debate that the modernist writers of the West were having at the beginning of the 20th century, about moving away from Symbolism for its simplicity and going on to more anarchic literary devices, stream-of-consciousness and all that. But there is merit in the simplicity and in the complexity, and in this film more than any other I felt that Ghatak managed to bridge the two and made something unforgettable. It filled me with the horror I felt after first watching Apocalypse Now without the hungama. I feel like I sound like an idiot, but there is something so complete about the way Ghatak tells stories that it feels impossible to build upon, or improve. It feels like this is the last story to ever be told.
